summary: Proposes a protocol for connecting host computers to ARPA-like networks through directly connected front end processors. It offers approaches using available hardware and software and acknowledges many contributors.

eli5.summary: Instead of making every big computer learn the network rules, a smaller helper machine takes care of it. This proposes how they should talk.

rigid vs flexible front end arpanet
subtitle: A 1974 proposal to attach hosts to ARPA-like networks through a small front end that speaks a five-command protocol.

tldr.problem: Many organizations planned to attach computers with no ARPANET counterpart to ARPA-like networks, and writing a Network Control Program (NCP) for a new system is a major undertaking.
tldr.mechanism: A small front-end machine handles the NCP and talks to the host over a compact Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP) of five commands, rather than pretending to be a known device such as a remote job entry station.
tldr.outcome: The authors recommend this flexible front end over the rigid known-device approach and describe the protocol as around 90% complete. The unit metadata lists the status as Unknown.

today: RFC 647 is a 1974 proposal whose status is listed as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It describes a protocol proposal, and the text does not say whether it was adopted.

sections.title: Two Ways to Front-End a Host
sections.content:
In fall 1974 a large number of organizations planned to attach general purpose computers to the ARPANET or to interconnect systems using "ARPANET technology". Many of those systems had no ARPANET counterpart, so special hardware interfaces and NCPs could not simply be copied. The document puts it plainly: designing an NCP for a new system is a major undertaking.

The shared model is Host *** Front End --- IMP --- Network: a small machine, a PDP-11 being widely held most suitable, sits between the IMP and the host to shield it from the NCP. The proposal assumes the ELF system on the front end, noting ANTS would serve too. The open question is what happens at the asterisks.
sections.eli5: A little helper computer stands between the big computer and the network. The question is how the big computer should talk to the helper.

sections.title: Rigid Versus Flexible
sections.content:
The popular rigid approach has the front end simulate a known device, typically a remote job entry station like the CDC 200UT, so the host needs no software changes. The authors object that the host can then handle network data only in ways it already handles that device, so a simulated card reader means batch input. They cite lost functionality (teleconferencing and graphics are examples), mismatched speeds (a 4800 baud line against a 50,000 baud subnet), and an anecdote of a PDP-15 front end where Telnet terminal-type questions went wrong.

Their flexible alternative drops the "no host changes" goal for MINIMAL changes: attach the front end to any convenient high-speed channel, let it handle the NCP, and define a compact protocol, the H-FP, whose host module distributes data inside the operating system. They estimate a minimal H-FP routine takes the same few man-months as a known-device simulation package.
sections.eli5: The rigid way makes the helper pretend to be an old card reader, so the big computer can only do old things. The flexible way teaches the big computer a tiny new language so it can do much more.

sections.title: The H-FP Commands
sections.content:
All communication is in terms of five commands, and either side may send any of them. The first byte of each command carries its number, and a byte is a per-installation width such as 8, 9 or 12 bits. A connection is identified by an INDEX; INDEX 0 is the global connection between host and front end, and each side sends a BEGIN for it when it comes up.

BEGIN carries INDEX, HOST, SOCKET, TRANSLATION-TYPE and CONNECTION-TYPE. SOCKET 1 means Telnet, 3 means FTP, 5 means the ARPANET RJE protocol and 77 a host-specific RJE/batch connection. ACKNOWLEDGE must answer every command except another ACKNOWLEDGE, with CODE 0 for success and 1 for failure. MESSAGE carries data with a COUNT of bits. INTERRUPT maps to an NCP interrupt, such as a Telnet quit. END terminates a connection, with CODE 1 for a general close and 2 to 4 for a foreign system, foreign IMP or local IMP going down.
sections.eli5: There are only five kinds of note: "start a conversation", "got it", "here is some data", "interrupt", and "we are done".

sections.title: How Hosts Use It
sections.content:
The front end shields the host from NCP commands and sockets, and by default refuses negotiated Telnet options and strips Telnet control codes, optionally mapping ASCII to the host's character set. For file transfer, the host module must handle FTP stor and retr and can refuse BEGINs on socket 3 if it cannot. Flow control is just the ACKNOWLEDGE command, since the link is assumed short and fast.

A host can use the protocol fully, partially (accepting BEGINs on sockets 1 and 3 so the front end manages Telnet and FTP details), or minimally by accepting only the private connection on socket 77. Every level can be upgraded without changing the front end. The document also includes a personal appendix by the author, Appendix 2, on implementers, which the main argument does not depend on.
sections.eli5: A big computer can use the helper a lot, a little, or only for the basics, and it can start small and grow later.

items.label: BEGIN
items.desc: Opens a connection on an INDEX: host, socket, translation and connection type.

items.label: ACKNOWLEDGE
items.desc: Answers every other command with a success or failure code.

items.label: MESSAGE
items.desc: Carries COUNT bits of data on an INDEX.

items.label: INTERRUPT
items.desc: Maps to an NCP interrupt for the process on an INDEX.

items.label: END
items.desc: Terminates a connection, with a reason code.
